subject: bicycle
pitch: A vintage Dutch city bicycle in mint green. Tall upright handlebars with cream grips and a silver bell, a brown leather saddle with springs, chrome mudguards, a chain guard, a wicker basket on the front filled with sunflowers and a baguette, and whitewall tyres.
reasoning:
I need to write a single TypeScript module, being careful since I'm not fully certain of the exact SDK signatures for builder parts like position, bone attachment, and orientation options, so I'll stick to the safer, more commonly documented usage patterns.

Rather than relying on uncertain helper functions for connecting joints, I'll build my own cylinder-based helper that orients geometry between two points using quaternions, then attach it via the builder's part function with a bone reference. For the actual skeleton, I'm planning a minimal bicycle structure with a frame root joint and child joints for the fork/headset, both wheels, crank, and pedals, using parent references between joint objects, and sizing the wheels around a realistic 28-inch radius.

Now I'm working out wheel geometry: positioning the axles at a 1.1 wheelbase along +Z, building the tyre as a torus rotated into the wheel plane, and figuring out how to layer thin cream rings onto the black tyre torus to create a whitewall effect using offset ring geometries along the torus's side curvature.

Positioning the rings...

Now I'm planning the chrome rim as a thin torus, with spokes as cylinders running from hub to rim, offset slightly to create a crossing pattern. I'm also sketching a helper function to build and align a rod between two points, assuming part placement works in model-space coordinates with a default origin when no explicit position is passed.

Switching to the frame geometry, I'm laying out a Dutch-style bike in mint green, defining key points for the rear axle, bottom bracket, seat tube, head tube, and top/down tubes to get that classic upright gents frame with a slanted seat tube and nearly horizontal top tube.

Now I'm adding chainstays and seatstays connecting to the rear axle, then working out the fork geometry—tilt angle, crown position, and steering joint placement so the fork, handlebars, basket, and front wheel can all pivot together as a child hierarchy under the steering axis.

Continuing to the handlebars, I'm sketching out a Dutch-style swept-back bar path from the stem through a few waypoints to the grips, planning to build it from simple rod segments joined by spheres rather than a continuous curve, with cream-colored grip cylinders at the ends and a bell mounted near the right side of the bar.

For the bell I'm using a small hemispherical chrome dome with a little lever on top, and considering adding a small front lamp near the crown for detail. Then I'm working out the front basket: a tapered wicker-colored frustum sitting above the front wheel, with torus rings for woven texture, positioned to avoid clashing with the head tube by nudging it further forward and shrinking its radius slightly, and supported by rods running down to the fork crown.

Now I'm filling the basket with sunflowers, building a reusable helper that constructs each flower's disc and petals locally then transforms them into position with rotation and translation matrices -- centers, brown cylinder discs, and rings of petals angled outward to look like flowers nestled in the basket.

With the flowers placed, stems and leaves run from the basket rim up to each flower head, oriented via quaternions pointing from "up" to the flower's facing direction. Then I move on to a baguette: a tilted capsule shape sticking forward-left out of the basket, positioned and angled so it clears the handlebars, with small darker slanted marks suggesting the scored crust.

Now I'm working on the rear mudguard, considering whether to build it from a partial torus or a partial open cylinder to get that curved chrome fender look, weighing tradeoffs around culling and visibility from inside the arc.

Working out the axis rotation for the cylinder geometry...

So θ=90° is top, θ=180° is rear. I want the fender to span roughly from just above the front of the wheel (θ~15°) over the top and down toward the rear (θ~170°), covering the arc the rear wheel would kick up debris from.

Adjusting the rear fender to run from about 20° to 190°, and the front fender to span roughly -20° to 110° so it curves from below horizontal in front over the top. I'm checking that the winding stays consistent after rotation, and since fender radius .365 is bigger than tyre radius .346, it'll clear properly—I'll add small support rods connecting fender to axle, and maybe a tiny red reflector at the rear fender's tail end. For the chain guard, I'm thinking a flat cover on the right side where the chain typically runs.

For the Dutch-style chain case, I'm building a stadium-like shape—big disc at the crank, small disc at the rear hub, tapering slab between them—defining it as a 2D shape with an arc around the crank and a line to the rear circle, then extruding it along the frame axis.

Still mapping arm shape...

Placing the crank arms vertically with the right arm swinging down to the pedal and the left arm up to its pedal, sizing the pedal boxes and the chrome bottom bracket axle cylinder, then moving on to position the seat post rising from the seat tube.

Continuing the seat post direction up to a saddle position, I'm planning a brown leather saddle connected to the post by two coil springs, and I'm defining a helix curve class to generate the spring geometry as a thin tube.

Placing the springs near the rear and nose of the saddle, I'm building the saddle shape itself using two scaled spheres—a wider one for the rear and a narrower one for the nose—to approximate the classic saddle silhouette.

Lowering saddle to 1.03 with springs around .95-.99, and reworking seat tube, top tube, head tube, and down tube coordinates so the frame geometry stays proportional and the fork crown aligns properly with the head tube angle.

I'll bend the fork blades with a kinked midpoint to get that curved rake look, then set the head tube endpoints and run the steering axis up through a tall stem to the handlebar position, typical of a Dutch bike's upright geometry.

Now I'm plotting the handlebar sweep -- going outward, then curving back and up into the grips, mirrored on both sides -- and adding small brake lever rods under the grips while skipping the cable detail. I'm placing a small headlamp near the fork crown but deciding to leave it out for now to keep things simple.

I'm positioning a chrome bell near the left grip, sizing its dome and clamp, and figuring out the basket's dimensions -- center height, taper from bottom to top radius, and making sure its back edge and the flowers above it don't collide with the handlebars or the front wheel's top edge.

Now I'm detailing the basket construction: a torus rim at the top, woven bands made of slightly darker tori at intervals down the slanted wall, and a ring of thin vertical rods connecting the bottom radius to the top radius for the woven texture, plus support rods running from the basket's base.

I'll also consider steering supports connecting the basket to the handlebar stem, and whether to add a leather strap or a rear rack platform above the rear fender for authenticity, though I may skip these as optional extras.

I'm deciding to skip the kickstand since the bike rests on its wheels, and now I'm setting up the joint structure—placing the root frame joint at the bounding box, with child joints for the rear wheel and crank positioned accordingly, with unbonned parts attaching to the nearest bone automatically.

I'm figuring out the steering joint and front wheel placement as children of the frame hierarchy, and considering whether to use a parent-joint reference versus naming conventions for attaching parts to specific bones. Wheel spin will just rotate around the x-axis, so the joint's default orientation shouldn't matter there.

Now I'm designing a wheel-building function that layers a tyre torus with whitewall and chrome rim rings, a hub cylinder, and 28 laced spokes running from hub to rim using thin rod cylinders -- roughly 56 spoke parts total across both wheels.

Defining the frame tube geometry...

Working out the fender geometry as a partial open cylinder arc, deciding on the angular span so it wraps the wheel without clashing with the dropout, and considering whether to leave it single-sided since the interior shouldn't be visible from typical viewing angles.

Working out torus scaling for the fender band...

Setting the front fender arc from 35° to 200° with radius .37, checking clearance against the tire's outer radius and width. Now I'm working out the stay rods connecting the fork crown to the fender, positioning them at specific angles so the fender attaches realistically above the tire.

For the rear fender, I'm centering it at a different point along the wheelbase, starting the arc near -10° and sweeping roughly 175° to wrap over the rear tire toward the seat area.

Checking the reflector placement near the fender tail and confirming the bike's overall length and wheelbase stay consistent, then placing a small red reflector box toward the rear. I'm also sketching in a simple rear rack positioned above the fender, adjusting its height so it doesn't collide with the seat tube or saddle.

Now I'm working out the rack geometry: rods running along the frame axis, cross bars, and diagonal stays connecting to the rear axle and seatstay, checking each point stays clear of the tire and fender. I'm picking a dark grey color for the rack and planning a small helix spring component with modest turns and radius.

For the saddle, I'm setting leather tones for the seat and piping, adding a chrome seat post sized to match the seat tube's slope with a small collar clamp at the top, and starting on the saddle rails extending from the nose.

Still working out saddle geometry...

Now I'm checking handlebar height relative to the saddle, raising the stem and bars so they sit higher like a typical Dutch bike setup, then plotting out the curved path points for the bar shape.

Placing grips, cream rubber with end caps, chrome bar sections and joint spheres, plus a brake lever rod. I'm adding a bell on the left side of the bar with a dome, collar, and striker, then starting on the basket support rods running back to the stem.

Now scattering five sunflowers around the basket rim at varied positions and tilt directions, each roughly .085 in radius and spaced so they overlap slightly but still read as distinct blooms, with stems still to come.

Adding leaves as flattened green spheres near the rim with slight random yaw rotation, then defining the sunflower materials: yellow petals, darker inner petal shade, and a brown disc center with a darker ring, built from a short cylinder plus a flattened dome.

Still writing geometry transforms...

Now I'm figuring out where to place the baguette relative to the basket and flowers, computing a base position and direction vector so it sticks up and forward without colliding with the handlebars.

I notice the baguette's path crosses too close to one of the flowers (F2), so I need to shift that flower slightly to avoid the overlap.

Still placing flower coordinates...

Now I'm working out the small decorative boxes for the slash marks—sizing thin rectangular geometries and rotating them around the local Y axis to get a diagonal crosshatch look on the surface.

For the basket, I'm thinking through a woven frustum form with torus rings at varying heights and radii for the weave pattern, a darker rim torus at top, and a base disc — but I need to handle the open cylinder's face culling issue so the inner wall is visible too, likely by adding a flipped inner geometry.

For wicker texture I'll add vertical staves in a lighter tone with horizontal torus bands wrapping around. I'll skip the lamp and kickstand, but add chrome headset rings at the head tube ends using short rod cylinders, plus pedals as dark boxes with chrome accents and a crank joint positioned at the bottom bracket. For the chainring I'm placing a cream/chrome disc just inside the guard, offset slightly along the x-axis so it sits properly nested.

I'm adding a chrome chainring and dark thin chain rods connecting it to the rear sprocket, visible through the gap near the chainstays on the inside face, along with a rear sprocket cylinder sized to match. I'm working out the guard's hub position and bottom bracket coordinates to make sure everything lines up correctly in y and z.

I'm extruding the guard shape and positioning it next to the frame, and double-checking that the tire radius places the wheel bottom close enough to the ground. Now I'm setting up wire spokes with a chrome material color.

Setting up build script joints...

Still defining placement helpers and the wheel geometry function...

Still designing wheel geometry...

Writing flip helper and curve class...

I'm defining a Helix curve class for the spring geometry, then building a sunflower placement function that orients geometry along a direction vector using quaternions, and sketching out the disc, dome, and petal cone shapes for the flower head.

Finishing the petal orientation with scale and translation, I'm moving on to leaves, stem rods connecting the basket to flowers, and a baguette shape built from capsule geometry with scoring cuts. I'm making sure everything attaches to the right joints (steering vs frame) before writing out the final part counts for spokes and flowers.

Now I'm constructing the basket weave with vertical rods and horizontal torus bands around a cylindrical core, mirroring left-right symmetric parts, then starting the bike fork with a steering crown box and blade rods.

Continuing to position the fork blades, axle hub, and dropout tip, then adding the front axle cap and rear chainstay positions to complete the frame geometry.
